1.pericope_label: And Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in peace to Jerusalem. And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the Lord? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the Lord. Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God.

schools.summary: Ellicott notices that the wording suggests a contrast with the fate of Ahab and would render in peace as in wholeness or soundness, that is unhurt. He identifies Jehu as the son of the seer who had suffered for his reproof of Asa and had himself already witnessed against the king of Israel, and draws the point that the prophets never shrank from facing the highest representatives of earthly power. He renders the charge as an infinitive, oughtest thou to help, with the ungodly as the emphatic word, and turns the second clause into a question of its own, and haters of the Lord lovest thou, the particle before haters being characteristic of the chronicler's style. On the threatened wrath he raises a problem of comparison, since the same phrase is used of David where the wrath was embodied in pestilence, and asks what form it took here, thinking the following chapters supply the answer beginning with the invasion of the land; and he glosses the mitigation as meaning the wrath will not pursue him to destruction because there are good things found in him.

Gill notes from the family connection that the imprisonment of Jehu's father for reproving Asa did not deter his son, and reads the good things found in Jehoshaphat as principles of grace and righteousness and holiness from which many good works sprang.

Clarke says only that Jehoshaphat was safe notwithstanding a danger so imminent that none but the especial mercy of God could have saved him, and then presses the application rather than the history, asking whether the wrath of God is not upon all alliances his people form with the ungodly, whether social, matrimonial, commercial or political. Wesley answers Ellicott's question with three instances, that God chastised Jehoshaphat partly by stirring up the Moabites and others to invade him, partly by permitting his eldest son to kill all his brothers, and principally by bringing an almost general destruction on his grandchildren, which he calls the fruit of the alliance with Ahab; and he reads the good things as good marks from an honest heart, which God regards more than this particular error, so that he will chasten but not destroy.

Henry measures the safe return against three worse outcomes, that Jehoshaphat fared better than he expected, having been in imminent peril and yet coming home in peace; better than he deserved, having been out of the way of his duty on an expedition he could not account for to God and his conscience, since God is not extreme to mark what we do amiss nor withdraw his protection the moment we forfeit it; and better than Ahab, who was brought home slain, two kings being in the field together, one taken and the other left. On the reproof he notes that Jehu's father was an eminent prophet in the last reign, as appeared by Asa putting him in the stocks for his plain dealing, and that the son was not afraid to reprove another king, and he puts the charge as two questions, whether a godly man should help the ungodly by giving them a hand of fellowship and lending them a hand of assistance, and whether he should love those whom God beholds afar off.

debates: What form the threatened wrath took, which Ellicott raises as a problem by comparison with the pestilence sent on David and refers forward to the following chapters, and which Wesley answers with three specific judgments ending in the destruction of Jehoshaphat's grandchildren.

Why Jehoshaphat was spared at all when Ahab was killed, where Henry makes it a distinguishing mercy shown to one who had said he was as Ahab was, and Clarke makes it simply the especial mercy of God in an imminent danger.

What the reproof is for, which Clarke generalises into a question about every alliance God's people form with the ungodly, social, matrimonial, commercial or political, while the others keep it to this particular expedition.
outliers: Ellicott draws from Jehu's errand the general point that the prophets never shrank from facing the highest representatives of earthly power.
Henry holds that whenever we return in safety we ought to acknowledge God's providence over our going out and coming in, and the more so when kept through more than ordinary dangers.
themes: And Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in peace to Jerusalem.

And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the Lord? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the Lord.
Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God.

4.pericope_label: And Jehoshaphat dwelt at Jerusalem: and he went out again through the people from Beer–sheba to mount Ephraim, and brought them back unto the Lord God of their fathers. And he set judges in the land throughout all the fenced cities of Judah, city by city, And said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the Lord, who is with you in the judgment. Wherefore now let the fear of the Lord be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that the king went in person, holding that he went out by his accredited representatives, and treats the journey as a second visitation after the earlier commission for instructing the people in the law. He is precise about what the people were brought back from, not only the Baals but the illicit worship of Jehovah itself, and quotes an account of how the two had assimilated, the local worship of the God of Israel necessarily coming into contact with the Canaanite service of Baal and the offerings of Jehovah, consecrating the good things of his bestowing, being in a land of corn and wine no longer the scanty products of pastoral life. On the charge he renders the first motive as a denial, that it is not for man they will judge but for Jehovah as his vicegerents, and the second as a promise of presence; he notes that the Greek and Latin misunderstand the clause while the Syriac has them be strong and judge true judgment; and he closes with two observations, that those who judge for Jehovah are bound to judge like Jehovah, and that the king's own name means Jehovah judgeth.
Gill reads the opening clause as a withdrawal, that Jehoshaphat went out no more to Samaria nor concerned himself with the affairs of Israel but attended to his own.

Clarke takes the boundary formula as evidence that Jehoshaphat made the circuit in person, since before the separation the extent of the land was given as from Dan to Beer-sheba while Judah was now bounded south by Beer-sheba and north by the mountains of Ephraim, so the phrase shows he had gone through all his territories to examine everything himself; on the charge to the judges he puts the whole matter in one line, that judges should feel themselves in the place of God and judge as those who know they shall be judged for their judgments. Wesley supplies the motive the others leave out and connects the reform to the rebuke, since many had probably revolted to idolatry on seeing their king so intimate with idolaters and Jehoshaphat therefore thought himself doubly obliged to reduce them, from which Wesley draws the rule that if we truly repent of sin we shall do our utmost to repair the damage we have done to religion or to the souls of others.

Henry sets the judicial reform beside the earlier teaching mission, since having sent preachers to instruct the people Jehoshaphat now saw it requisite to send judges to see the laws put in execution and be a terror to evil-doers, and supposes there were judges before whom either neglect or popular contempt had made useless, so the institution had to be new-modelled with new men and a new charge. He divides the charge into two means and three motives: the means are great caution, since judges of all men have need of it because so much depends on the correctness of their judgment, and great piety, the fear of God being both a restraint and an engagement to activity; the motives are that from God they had their commission, that his eye is upon them in the judgment, and that he is the great example of justice, there being no bribery nor respect of persons with him.

debates: Whether Jehoshaphat made the circuit himself, which Clarke infers from the boundary formula and Ellicott denies, holding that he went out by his accredited representatives.
What the people were brought back from, where Ellicott insists it was not only the Baals but an illicit worship of Jehovah that had assimilated to them, while the others take it as plain idolatry.

Why the reform was undertaken when it was, which Wesley traces to the king's own example having driven men to idolatry, so that the reform was reparation, while Henry treats it as the natural completion of the earlier teaching mission.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the king's own name, Jehoshaphat, denotes Jehovah judgeth, and that those who judge for Jehovah are bound to judge like Jehovah.
Henry holds that if destruction from God is a terror to the judges, they will be a terror to none but evil-doers.

8.pericope_label: Moreover in Jerusalem did Jehoshaphat set of the Levites, and of the priests, and of the chief of the fathers of Israel, for the judgment of the Lord, and for controversies, when they returned to Jerusalem. And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the Lord, faithfully, and with a perfect heart. And what cause soever shall come to you of your brethren that dwell in their cities, between blood and blood, between law and commandment, statutes and judgments, ye shall even warn them that they trespass not against the Lord, and so wrath come upon you, and upon your brethren: this do, and ye shall not trespass. And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the Lord; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king’s matters: also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and the Lord shall be with the good.

schools.summary: Ellicott describes the institution rather than its constitution, a high court of appeal in the capital such as Deuteronomy prescribes, with the high priest naturally president in spiritual cases and the tribal prince in civil ones and the Levites as writers, inferior officials such as scribes and notaries acting under their direction. He keeps the received reading of the clause about returning and refers it to the earlier royal commission, placing a full stop at controversies and noting that the Syriac and Arabic begin the clause there. He argues the high priest's identity from chronology, Amariah standing fifth from Zadok in the genealogy as Jehoshaphat was the fifth king from David. On the duty of warning he has the judges teach the parties the true sense of the law in the particular case so they do not incur guilt by false judgment, and observes that a miscarriage of justice would involve not the immediate agents only but the whole people in guilt and its penal consequences.

Gill reads it as a single body, the great court of judicature consisting of princes, priests and Levites, of ecclesiastics and political persons together, since causes of both sorts were brought there.

Clarke is most definite that there were two jurisdictions, ecclesiastical and civil, the high priest supreme judge in one and Zebadiah in the other with the Levites as counsellors to both, and presses it as a principle that the things of God and the things of the king should never be confounded in the administration of justice. On the clause about returning to Jerusalem he raises a textual objection, that if the text spoke of anyone returning the preposition would be used and it is not, and reports with approval the conjecture that the word should read not and they returned but the inhabitants. He divides the matters concretely, taking the questions of blood as cases of manslaughter or of consanguinity and inheritance and those of law and commandment as whatever concerns the moral precepts and ceremonies or belongs to civil affairs. Wesley declines to settle the constitution of the court, finding it not easy to determine whether these made up one court deciding all causes or two distinct courts.

Henry takes it for one court with a divided presidency, Amariah presiding in ecclesiastical causes and being last consulted in cases the judges themselves doubted of, and Zebadiah as prime minister presiding in all civil causes. He explains why homicide came to Jerusalem, since after the revolt all the cities of refuge except Hebron belonged to the northern kingdom, so the courts of the temple or the horns of the altar were chiefly used as sanctuaries and the trial of homicides was reserved for the capital. He closes on the division of labour with evident pleasure, that some best understand the matters of the Lord and others the king's matters and neither can say to the other that it has no need of him, there being diversities of gifts but all from the same Spirit, and blesses God both for magistrates and ministers, scribes and statesmen, men of books and men of business.

debates: Whether Jehoshaphat set up one court in Jerusalem or two, where Clarke holds for two separate jurisdictions, Gill for one mixed body, Henry for one court with a divided presidency, and Wesley finds the question not easy to determine.

How the clause about returning to Jerusalem should be read, where Clarke objects that the preposition is missing and prefers a conjectural reading giving the inhabitants of Jerusalem, while Ellicott keeps the text and refers the return to the earlier royal commission.
Which Amariah is meant, which Ellicott settles by chronology, since he stands fifth from Zadok as Jehoshaphat was the fifth king from David.
outliers: Clarke holds that without good and wholesome laws no nation can be prosperous, and that the best laws are vain if they are not judiciously and conscientiously administered.
Ellicott observes that a miscarriage of justice would involve not the judges only but the whole people in guilt and its penal consequences.
themes: Moreover in Jerusalem did Jehoshaphat set of the Levites, and of the priests, and of the chief of the fathers of Israel, for the judgment of the Lord, and for controversies, when they returned to Jerusalem.
And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the Lord, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.

And what cause soever shall come to you of your brethren that dwell in their cities, between blood and blood, between law and commandment, statutes and judgments, ye shall even warn them that they trespass not against the Lord, and so wrath come upon you, and upon your brethren: this do, and ye shall not trespass.
